summary: Sirach 16 begins by warning that many children are no security if they are ungodly, while one person with understanding can matter greatly. The chapter then recalls examples of divine judgment, insists that mercy and correction both belong to God, rejects the idea that a person can be hidden in a vast creation, and ends by pointing to the ordered works of creation.
whyItMatters: This chapter joins ordinary family hopes, moral accountability, and the scale of creation into one lesson about wisdom under God. It also shows Sirach’s habit of moving from practical counsel to theological reflection without treating either as separate from disciplined living.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the Greek translation was made by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal learning, and Jewish life taking place within a Greek-speaking Mediterranean world.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in compact poetic teaching, using direct address, maxims, examples, and reflection on creation.

outline.heading: Children without wisdom
outline.note: The teacher says that many ungodly children are not better than one person with understanding.

outline.heading: Judgment remembered
outline.note: Past examples of sinners, a disobedient nation, the giants of old time, Lot’s neighbors, and hardened people are used as warnings.

outline.heading: Mercy and correction
outline.note: God is described as mighty to forgive and also as one who judges each person according to works.

outline.heading: Unprinted verses
outline.note: The World English Bible leaves these verse numbers blank.

outline.heading: No one hidden
outline.note: The chapter rejects the thought that a person is too small to be remembered within boundless creation.

outline.heading: Ordered creation
outline.note: The teacher calls the student to listen and points to the Lord’s ordered works, the earth’s blessings, and living things that return to it.

keyVerses.text: Don’t trust in their life. Don’t rely on their numbers; for one can be better than a thousand, and to die childless than to have ungodly children.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the opening warning: numerical increase is not the same as wisdom or faithfulness.

keyVerses.text: As his mercy is great, so is his correction also. He judges a man according to his works.
keyVerses.why: This sentence holds together the chapter’s paired stress on mercy and accountability.

keyVerses.text: Don’t say, “I will be hidden from the Lord,” and “Who will remember me from on high?” I will not be known among so many people, for what is my soul in a boundless creation?
keyVerses.why: This introduces the objection the chapter answers: that an individual life might be too small for divine notice.

keyVerses.text: In the judgment of the Lord are his works from the beginning. From the making of them he determined their boundaries.
keyVerses.why: This begins the closing reflection on creation as ordered under God’s judgment and boundaries.

questions.question: Why does the chapter speak so sharply about children?
questions.answer: The opening does not treat children as a simple measure of blessing. It warns that a large family without “the fear of the Lord” is not something to rely on. In this chapter, moral formation matters more than numbers.

questions.question: What does “unprofitable children” mean here?
questions.answer: The phrase is used alongside “ungodly sons” and children who lack “the fear of the Lord.” In context, “unprofitable” is not about economic productivity but about a life that does not embody wisdom or reverence. The chapter contrasts such children with “one who has understanding.”

questions.question: Is the chapter saying childlessness is always better?
questions.answer: No. The comparison is limited: “to die childless” is said to be better than having “ungodly children.” The point is not a general rule against children, but a warning that family size does not replace wisdom or reverence.

questions.question: Who are the “giants of old time” and “Lot’s neighbors”?
questions.answer: The chapter names them as examples of people not spared when they revolted, acted proudly, or sinned. It alludes to their stories without retelling them in detail. They function here as remembered warnings about strength, pride, and judgment.

questions.question: How can mercy and wrath both be with God in this chapter?
questions.answer: Verse 11 says “mercy and wrath are both with him who is mighty to forgive,” and verse 12 adds that mercy and correction are both great. The chapter does not present mercy as denial of accountability. It describes God as able to forgive and also as judging “according to his works.”

questions.question: Why are verses 15 and 16 blank in this edition?
questions.answer: The World English Bible leaves verses 15 and 16 blank. Sirach survives in different textual forms, and editions can differ in wording and verse numbering. Other editions may include additional lines or number the passage differently.

questions.question: What mistaken thought is being challenged in verse 17?
questions.answer: The speaker challenges the idea that someone can be hidden from the Lord because creation is so vast and the person seems insignificant. The quoted thought asks, “Who will remember me from on high?” The following verses answer by describing heaven, earth, mountains, and foundations as responsive when God visits or looks.

questions.question: Does the chapter claim people can fully understand God’s ways?
questions.answer: No. It asks, “Who could comprehend his ways?” and compares many works to a tempest that no one can see. The chapter holds together two claims: God’s works are ordered and real, yet many of them remain hidden from human understanding.

questions.question: Why does the chapter end by talking about creation?
questions.answer: After warning against foolish thoughts about being hidden, the teacher turns the student toward instruction and the ordered works of the Lord. Creation is described as bounded, arranged, obedient, blessed, and filled with living things. This gives scale to the chapter’s earlier claim that human lives are not outside divine attention.

glossary.def: A phrase in this chapter for the reverent orientation that should be present in children if their increase is to be a cause for delight.
A person described as stubbornly resistant; in this chapter, even one such person is not assumed to escape punishment.
The vast creation named in the objection that one individual might be hidden or forgotten.
The chapter uses this word both for human deeds, according to which a person is judged, and for the Lord’s ordered acts in creation.
